title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM-Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared-Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment evaluating whether coupling a single LLM (gpt-5-mini) with a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, single automated repair attempt, shared_initial_candidate semantics) reduces unsafe intent‑to‑configuration proposals relative to the same initial LLM candidate observed without gating. Using a fixed deterministic task index (n=200 paired intents) drawn from a synthetic intent corpus and a Batfish‑style deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) in a sandbox, every paired episode produced a valid configuration under both baseline (LLM‑alone) and guarded conditions (n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered confirmatory estimand (paired difference in unsafe‑proposal rate) was 0.0 (exact two‑sided p=1.0). Exploratory diagnostics show no automated repairs were applied and median latencies were dominated by the shared initial generation. Baseline and guarded conditions reused the identical sampled initial candidate (shared_initial_candidate), therefore the confirmatory estimand measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and does not measure effects of independent guarded-conditioned regenerations or prompt-template interventions. We report the full preregistered design, execution manifest, and analysis. Interpretation: under the selected synthetic tasks, model, and strict shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded validator pipeline did not change outcomes because the initial candidates were already valid; this null result neither proves universal equivalence nor contradicts prior work showing validators can reduce hallucinations in other settings. We discuss construct, internal, external, and conclusion‑validity limitations and outline targeted next steps.

sections.introduction: Motivation: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks (intent‑to‑configuration translation, runbook generation, limited self‑healing). Prior surveys and empirical work emphasize that operational reliability depends heavily on system‑level guardrails—retrieval, validators, and assurance contracts—rather than the model alone [1],[2],[3]. Research gap: there is limited published, reproducible paired evidence comparing an identical LLM initial candidate observed without gating versus that same candidate after a deterministic verifier+gate under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Research question (confirmatory): Compared to LLM‑alone generation, does coupling the LLM with a deterministic verifier and deterministic accept/reject gate (with a single bounded automated repair attempt) reduce unsafe network‑change proposals on a fixed paired intent set? Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired design and frozen execution; (2) an autonomous run (n=200 paired intents) using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic Batfish‑style validator; (3) confirmatory and exploratory analyses and an evidence‑grounded discussion of implications and limitations.
sections.related_work: LLM use in NetOps and AIOps has rapidly expanded with work on intent‑based translation, runbook generation, and agentic NetOps; recent surveys highlight hallucination risks and the centrality of surrounding machinery (RAG, validators, contracts) for operational trustworthiness [1],[2],[3]. Deterministic validators and generate–validate–repair architectures are advocated in NetOps and adjacent domains (automated program repair, safety‑critical agents) as practical paths to safer automation [4],[5]. Empirical AIOps/DevOps reports show retrieval plus command‑safety checkers reduce unsafe command emissions but do not guarantee zero hallucination [6]. The literature also identifies gaps in validator‑coupled, reproducible NetOps benchmarks and paired experimental designs that measure validator effects under controlled semantics [7],[8].
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: We preregistered study autocand_A1_prereg_v1 before execution. Key frozen choices: model = gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses), generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial LLM candidate shared across paired conditions), task_count = 200 paired intents, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1, deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Sampling and tasks: 200 intents were selected deterministically from a synthetic intent generator covering VLAN migrations, failover workflows, and MTU upgrades; selection followed the adapter's deterministic index rule and was fixed prior to model calls. Primary metric and estimand: binary unsafe_flag (any reachability or policy violation reported by the validator); primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (difference in unsafe‑proposal rate between guarded and baseline conditions on paired units). Analysis plan: registered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor (exact McNemar‑equivalent), two‑sided alpha=0.05; failed‑call policy: complete_pair_primary (drop pair on unrecoverable infra failure); bootstrap CI computed with 10,000 resamples for paired bootstrap percentile intervals. Execution and constraints: runs were sandboxed (no live device changes); shared_initial_candidate semantics were enforced by the adapter so baseline and guarded arms observed the identical initial candidate per pair; therefore the confirmatory estimand measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and does not measure effects of independent guarded‑conditioned regenerations or prompt‑template interventions. Implementation: all raw responses, validator traces, repair logs, execution manifest, and model_configuration.json were archived and hashed; representative artifacts are provided in the evidence bundle.
sections.results: Execution summary: planned episodes = 400 (200 pairs), completed episodes = 400, failed episodes = 0, model_calls_used = 200 (shared initial generation per pair). Confirmatory outcome: complete_pair_count = 200; contingency table counts: n11 = 200 (both safe), n10 = 0 (guarded safe only), n01 = 0 (baseline safe only), n00 = 0 (both unsafe). Paired difference (guarded minus baseline) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). Interpretation of CI in context: the degenerate CI [0.0,0.0] reflects complete absence of discordant pairs under shared_initial_candidate semantics—i.e., every shared initial candidate was judged valid by the deterministic validator in both arms—so the experiment cannot reveal validator benefits for this sample. Exploratory diagnostics: repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes (no automated repairs triggered); validator reported valid = true for all final configurations. Latency: median end‑to‑end latency was dominated by the shared initial generation; guarded overhead was negligible because no repair attempts executed. Representative per‑task artifacts and validator traces (e.g., task‑000004) are archived in the evidence bundle.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and limitations of the null result: under the preregistered settings (single model, shared_initial_candidate, synthetic task generator, deterministic validator, single repair attempt), the guarded verifier pipeline did not change outcomes because the shared initial candidates generated by gpt‑5‑mini were valid for all sampled intents. This null result is a valid confirmatory outcome for the preregistered estimand and execution context but cannot generalize beyond those choices. Contributing factors likely include: (1) deterministic synthetic tasks and the chosen generator seed produced tasks with high baseline solvability; (2) shared_initial_candidate semantics precluded independent guarded‑conditioned regeneration; (3) a single strong LLM and conservative prompt profile produced high‑quality initial outputs; (4) validator rules aligned with the task generator's constraints. Relation to prior work: prior evaluations reporting verifier or RAG benefits typically allow guarded‑conditioned or augmented generation or use task banks with higher baseline unsafe rates [4],[6]. Operational implication: detecting verifier value experimentally requires task banks with nontrivial baseline unsafe rates or alternative execution semantics (e.g., independent guarded generation) and multi‑model evaluation. Recommendations for follow‑up experiments: (a) construct adversarial or OOD tasks to raise baseline unsafe rates; (b) add an explicit validator‑only arm and an independent guarded‑generation arm; (c) evaluate multiple LLMs and sampling settings; (d) execute in richer emulation environments and measure human‑in‑the‑loop interventions.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment comparing an LLM‑alone single‑shot outcome versus that same initial candidate after a deterministic verifier+gate with bounded automated repair. In this run (n=200 paired intents, gpt‑5‑mini, deterministic_netops_validator_v5, shared_initial_candidate semantics) every initial candidate was valid and the guarded verifier did not change any outcomes; the preregistered paired difference was 0.0. This null finding pertains strictly to the executed estimand and context. It underscores the necessity of careful construct design (task selection and generation semantics) for measurable evaluation of verifier benefits and provides an evidence‑grounded roadmap for focused next steps.

limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from the identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or prompt‑engineering differences.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability/policy rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions, vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point reductions but cannot rule out smaller effects in other contexts.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time, deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; the experiment did not evaluate retrieval‑based poisoning vectors (no RAG was used).
